title: Pushyavarman founds the Varman line
text: The first historical dynasty of Kamarupa begins, ruling from Pragjyotishpura. Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar names Kamarupa and Davaka as frontier kingdoms.

title: Davaka joins Kamarupa
text: By the later 5th century Davaka in the Kopili valley is no longer separate. Mahendravarman performs horse sacrifices claiming wide rule.

title: Bhutivarman's grant
text: Bhutivarman grants land in the Sylhet region (Chandrapuri), later renewed by Bhaskaravarman in the Nidhanpur plates.

title: Bhaskaravarman takes the throne
text: The greatest Varman king allies with Harsha of Kanauj against Shashanka of Gauda.

title: Xuanzang visits Kamarupa
text: The Chinese pilgrim stays at Bhaskaravarman's court and describes the kingdom as some 10,000 li around.

title: Victory camp at Karnasuvarna
text: The undated Nidhanpur charter names Bhaskaravarman’s victory camp at Karnasuvarna. The map uses c.643 as a reference year; the acquisition date and full extent of Gauda possession are uncertain.

title: Salastambha seizes the throne
text: With the Varman line extinct, a local chief founds the Mlechchha (Salastambha) dynasty.

title: Harjaravarman's Tezpur inscription
text: The rock inscription at Tezpur records Harjaravarman, the strongest king of the line, ruling from Haruppeswara.

title: Brahmapala elected
text: The nobles choose Brahmapala as king after Tyagasimha dies without an heir.

title: Chandra kings in Srihatta
text: Srichandra of Harikela grants land in Srihatta (Sylhet) in the Paschimbhag plate.

title: Kamarupa’s Pala succession becomes uncertain
text: The local Pala line gives way during the early12th century. Exact end date and the succession through Bengal intervention are disputed.

title: Bengal Pala intervention: approximate context
text: Ramapala’s intervention and the Tingyadeva–Vaidyadeva sequence are reconstructed from literary and epigraphic evidence.1110 is a display anchor; no exact conquest frontier is established.

title: Kamauli grant: one proposed CE date
text: Vaidyadeva’s regnal-year 4 charter is issued from Hamsakonci.1142 is the original editor’s preferred conversion;1123 is an alternative. Kamauli is the findspot near Varanasi, not his Assam capital.

title: Vallabhadeva’s endowment and genealogy
text: Saka 1107, conventionally 1185 (editor also allows 1184). Bhaskara, Rayarideva, Udayakarna and Vallabhadeva form a genealogy, not a dated reign list. Grant locality Kirtipur/Hapyacha is unresolved.

title: Traditional founding of the Chutia kingdom
text: Chutia tradition dates the founding by Birpal to 1187, in the far east of the valley.

title: Bakhtiyar’s disastrous return; defender unnamed
text: Kanai-Barashi-Bowa records destruction of invading Turks. The defender is not named; identification with Prithu is disputed. The inscription site is not a located battlefield.

title: Gachtal stone record and Visvasundara
text: Scholarship reads the stone inscription as Saka 1149/1227 and associates it with Visvasundara and temple restoration. It is distinct from the earlier Gachtal copper plates; identity with Prithu is disputed.

title: Sukaphaa reaches Assam
text: Sukaphaa enters the plains through the Patkai corridor and reaches the Namrup region in the conventional 1228 chronology. His settlement search precedes the Charaideo capital.

title: Samudrapala’s Ambari inscription
text: Saka 1154/1232 attests Samudrapala and mentions a royal-associated sattra at Yogihati. Its precise location and his reign boundaries remain unknown.

title: Sandhya: approximate reign context
text: Sandhya is conventionally dated c.1250–1270.1250 is a reconstruction anchor, not a dated accession inscription.

title: Charaideo becomes the Ahom capital
text: After moving between camps for 25 years, Sukaphaa settles at Charaideo.

title: Yuzbak defeated; Kamata transition follows
text: Yuzbak’s invasion ends in defeat and death, attributed to Sandhya’s resistance. The move to Kamatapur is generally placed after 1257, around 1260; the border switch this year is a display convention.

title: Approximate capital shift toward Kamatapur
text: The move from Kamarupanagara to Kamatapur is associated with Sandhya and often placed around 1260. The exact year remains uncertain.

title: The Dimasa at Dimapur
text: The Dimasa kingdom on the Dhansiri appears in Ahom chronicles; the Dikhow is the frontier.

title: Shah Jalal and the conquest of Sylhet
text: Gour Govinda, the last Gaur king of Sylhet, is defeated by the Bengal Sultanate's army with the Sufi Shah Jalal.

title: First Ahom–Kamata war
text: Sukhaangphaa's war with Kamata ends in a truce sealed by his marriage to the Kamata princess Rajani.

title: Ilyas Shah invades
text: Bengal forces occupy Kamrup including Guwahati; Kamata, Bhuyan and Barahi forces fight them on the Kopili.

title: Late-14th-century Chutia evidence
text: c.1380 is a display anchor, not a dated accession. The 1392 grant remembers Nandin and attests Satyanarayana’s Sadiya ruling genealogy.

title: Sudangphaa restores the Ahom throne
text: After long interregnums, a prince raised by a Brahmin family is enthroned. A 1401 treaty fixes the Patkai boundary.

title: The Khen dynasty
text: Niladhwaj founds the Khen dynasty at Kamatapur.

title: Husain Shah conquers Kamata
text: Kamatapur is besieged and destroyed; Nilambar is captured, ending the Khen dynasty.

title: The Jaintia kingdom
text: Traditional founding of the Jaintia kingdom, with its capital at Jaintiapur.

title: Local recovery after Bengal’s withdrawal
text: c.1505 is an approximate anchor for the recovery of independent chiefs after Bengal’s occupation; no single unified Bhuyan state is established by this date.

title: Biswa Singha founds the Koch kingdom
text: Conventional beginning of Biswa Singha’s dynasty from a small Chikna foothill base. Neighbouring-chief campaigns and movement into the plains form a gradual process; coronation dates vary between accounts.

title: Suhungmung annexes the Chutia kingdom
text: The decisive campaigns of c.1523–1524 end independent Chutia kingship; Sadiya comes under an Ahom governor. Last-king identities and death narratives differ between chronicles.

title: Dhansiri campaign against the Kacharis
text: A campaign against the Kacharis takes place in late 1526; renewed Marangi fighting follows in 1531. These events are separate from the 1523–1524 Chutia annexation.

title: First Muslim invasion of the Ahom kingdom
text: Suhungmung defeats the first of several invasions from Bengal (1527–1533), led by Turbak in 1532–33.

title: Renewed fighting at Marangi
text: Renewed Ahom–Kachari fighting in the Dhansiri region precedes the approximate 1532 settled-border stage used by this map.

title: Dimapur sacked
text: The Ahoms take Dimapur; the Dimasa move their capital to Maibong.

title: Nara Narayan and Chilarai
text: Nara Narayan inherits the western kingdom. Later campaigns under his brother Chilarai extend Koch influence; they do not all occur at his accession.

title: Pichala: the eastern advance is checked
text: The Koch advance toward Narayanpur fails at Pichala. The temporary eastern campaign layer ends after this setback; preparation precedes the renewed 1562 invasion.

title: Koch army takes Garhgaon
text: Koch forces occupy Garhgaon and Naranarayan camps at Majuli. The Majuli settlement requires Ahom submission and cession of north-bank land west of the Subansiri. Military presence on Majuli is distinct from permanent annexation of the island.

title: Rajmahal: Bengal’s sultanate falls
text: The formal Mughal province does not imply simultaneous conquest of Bhati, Sylhet and Chittagong.

title: The Koch kingdom splits
text: Nara Narayan grants the east to Chilarai's son Raghudev: Koch Bihar in the west, Koch Hajo in the east.

title: Bhati and the eastern delta submit
text: Eastern consolidation follows the earlier western victory.

title: Sylhet consolidated; Koch Hajo campaign opens
text: The western Assam campaign is staged separately from Bengal consolidation; dates vary between 1612 and 1613.

title: Koch Hajo annexed as Kamrup
text: Parikshit is defeated; Mughal administration is followed by resistance.

title: Resistance in annexed Kamrup
text: The conquest does not produce immediate uncontested possession.

title: First Mughal invasion: 1615–1616
text: The first invasion begins in 1615; the Ahom victory at Samdhara follows in 1616.

title: Samdhara and tributary Darrang
text: The first war ends in an Ahom victory; Balinarayan’s Darrang provides political reach toward Barnadi, distinct from direct annexation.

title: Pandu captured during a temporary advance
text: Gait dates the capture and fortification of Pandu to November 1617, followed by an unsuccessful attack on Hajo and retreat.

title: Asurar Ali: separate north and south boundaries
text: The 1639 agreement uses Barnadi on the north bank and Asurar Ali on the south, distinguishing the agreed frontier from earlier military reach.

title: Guwahati and Kamrup: 1658–1660
text: The map uses 1658 as a qualified annual anchor: Gait places the advance in the succession-war context; other accounts date Guwahati to 1659 and wider Kamrup to 1660.

title: Mir Jumla occupies Garhgaon
text: Aurangzeb's general takes the Ahom capital. Disease and the rains wreck his army.

title: Treaty of Ghilajharighat
text: The Ahoms cede land west of the Bharali and the Kolong and pay a heavy indemnity.

title: Chittagong conquered
text: The coastal addition is separate from the earlier delta consolidation; modern hill/princely districts are not blanket annexations.

title: Guwahati recovered
text: Lachit recovers Guwahati and Pandu and pushes the Mughal forces back toward Manas. Saraighat in 1671 defends this recovery.

title: Battle of Saraighat
text: Lachit Borphukan defeats Ram Singh's Mughal army in a river battle on the Brahmaputra at Guwahati.

title: Guwahati handed to the Mughals
text: In the turmoil of short reigns, Laluksola Borphukan surrenders Guwahati.

title: Battle of Itakhuli
text: Gadadhar Singha's army drives the Mughals out of Guwahati for good; the Manas becomes the frontier.

title: Rudra Singha's reign
text: The capital is set at Rangpur; Rudra Singha subdues the Dimasa (1706) and the Jaintia (1707).

title: The Dimasa move to Cachar
text: The Dimasa kingdom absorbs Koch Khaspur and moves its capital to Khaspur in the Cachar plains.

title: The East India Company gets the Diwani
text: With the Diwani of Bengal the Company takes over the revenue of Goalpara and Sylhet.

title: Company revenue authority
text: Bengal Diwani brings Company revenue authority in Goalpara and Sylhet. Revenue rights, military occupation and later district transfers are different changes.

title: The Moamoria rebellion
text: The followers of the Moamara satra rise against the Ahom state and take the capital Rangpur in 1769–1770 and again in the 1780s–1790s.

title: Captain Welsh's expedition
text: Gaurinath Singha asks the Company for help; Captain Thomas Welsh restores him (1792–1794). The capital moves to Jorhat.

title: The Matak territory
text: Kamaleswar Singha recognises the Matak leader Sarbananda Singha as Barsenapati of an autonomous territory.

title: Matak becomes autonomous
text: The 1805 settlement recognises Matak government under the Barsenapati within the Ahom political arrangement. The river-bounded country is shown separately from the Ahom realm.

title: Tripura becomes a British protectorate
text: NCERT dates protectorate status to 1809. The British-coloured hatch shows this relationship while local Manikya government continues. This is not a direct annexation of Hill Tippera into an Assam district.

title: First Burmese invasion
text: Invited by Badan Chandra Borphukan, a Burmese army enters Assam.

title: Burmese interventions begin
text: The 1817 and 1819 interventions precede the wider occupation from 1821. They do not begin a new British annexation.

title: Burmese occupation
text: Occupation and displacement begin in 1819. The annual map uses the 1825 recovery as the next territorial stage.

title: Burmese occupation
text: Chandrakanta Singha is driven out; the Burmese rule the valley through puppet kings.

title: Matak retains its own government
text: Matak’s chief protects the territory during the Burmese occupation elsewhere. Matak remains separately coloured from the occupied valley.

title: First Anglo-Burmese War
text: British troops enter Assam and take Guwahati in March 1824.

title: British advance into Assam
text: British forces occupy Lower Assam in 1824 and reach Rangpur in 1825. Campaign geography remains approximate; Matak’s local government is separate.

title: Gambhir Singh recovers Manipur
text: Recovery with British support is followed by the recognition provision at Yandabo. The map returns to Manipur’s own colour.

title: Treaty of Yandabo
text: 24 February: Ava renounces claims and interference regarding Assam, Cachar and Jaintia; the treaty includes a recognition provision for Gambhir Singh of Manipur. Matak and Sadiya retain separate local arrangements.

title: Yandabo; a separate Matak agreement
text: Ava renounces claims and interference regarding Assam at Yandabo on 24 February. A separate May 1826 engagement leaves the Barsenapati in local government with obligations to the Company.

title: Restored Manipur under British protection
text: Yandabo provides for Ava’s recognition of Gambhir Singh. The restored kingdom has British protection and political relations, shown with British-coloured hatching. This is different from direct British administration; the postwar 1891 settlement is a later stage.

title: Postwar Assam: different local arrangements
text: Company administration follows the war, but Matak and Sadiya retain separate local arrangements; Purandar’s restoration follows in 1833.

title: Anglo-Khasi war
text: The 1829–1833 war and agreements concern local states and British routes/stations. They are not one annexation of all present Meghalaya.

title: Cachar annexed
text: After Govindachandra's death the Cachar plains pass to the British.

title: Cachar plains annexed
text: The Cachar plains are annexed in 1832. Tularam’s hill territory remains separate, so the hills should not turn British with the plains.

title: Purandar Singha restored
text: The British make Purandar Singha tributary king of Upper Assam.

title: Purandar restored; Matak excluded
text: Purandar Singha receives a protected Upper Assam kingdom paying tribute. Matak and Sadiya remain excluded: this is not a reunion of Matak with his restored kingdom. North and south bank limits are approximate.

title: Khasi states and British relations
text: Local states and British station lands have different status. The dotted Khasi-region shape locates the states without turning the whole region into a directly administered British district.

title: Tularam’s territorial agreement
text: The October agreement reduces/redefines the retained hill territory. Its precise dividing line is not securely reconstructed here; the map preserves a qualified hill-region proxy instead of inventing a new border.

title: Kabaw boundary and compensation agreements
text: Separate agreements concern the Kabaw/Kubo Valley. The source collection is linked; no unsupported precise Kabaw polygon or popular “gift” narrative is added.

title: Jaintia annexed
text: The Jaintia kingdom is annexed by the British.

title: Matak’s tribute agreement changes
text: A January 1835 agreement substitutes tribute and a contingent obligation for the earlier arrangement. The Barsenapati continues local rule; no transfer to Purandar takes place.

title: Upper Assam annexed
text: Purandar Singha is removed and his restored territory passes to direct Company administration. Matak remains separate until direct management in 1839; a formal incorporation proclamation follows in 1842.

title: Purandar’s territory becomes directly British
text: Purandar is removed in 1838. The map shows the position after that year’s annexation: his restored territory becomes British, while Matak remains separately governed.

title: Tea in Assam
text: The Assam Company is formed; tea plantations spread across the valley.

title: Matak passes to direct Company management
text: After the Barsenapati’s death and rejection of revised terms by his successors, the Company assumes direct management. Sadiya’s rising and British intervention are a separate episode in the same year. This is incorporation under British rule, not Ahom reunion.

title: Formal incorporation of Matak and Sadiya
text: An 1842 proclamation formally incorporates both tracts into British territory and Lakhimpur district. The map remains British: the change is formal status after direct management began.

title: Tularam's hills annexed
text: After Tularam Senapati's death (1850) North Cachar is annexed.

title: Remaining hill territory annexed
text: The remaining Tularam hill territory passes into direct British administration. The separate Dimasa hill layer ends.

title: 1857 in Assam
text: The 1857 conspiracy/uprising in Assam precedes the executions of Maniram Dewan and Piyali Barua on 26 February 1858.

title: Maniram Dewan and Piyali Barua executed
text: 26 February 1858: executions at Jorhat following the 1857 conspiracy.

title: Naga Hills district formed
text: The district begins around the Angami/Doyang region with headquarters at Samaguting. Dotted modern-district proxies locate that stage; all present Nagaland is not annexed on this date.

title: Garo Hills district formed
text: A district is formed with headquarters at Tura. Some interior areas remain outside effective administration; dotted regional context distinguishes this from the later extension of control.

title: Lushai expedition
text: The 1871–1872 expedition is an earlier military intervention, distinct from permanent posts, formal annexation and the 1898 district merger.

title: British Political Agent in Tripura
text: Appointment of a resident Political Agent makes British oversight more explicit. Tripura is displayed as a princely state under British paramountcy, with the British hatch and its own local outline.

title: Garo Hills campaign
text: The 1872–1873 campaign extends administration into the interior. The map switches from district context to the approximate administered region in 1873.

title: Garo Hills brought under administration
text: The regional Garo layer becomes British after the campaign. Modern district contours are an approximation of the region, not the surveyed 1873 boundary.

title: A province of its own
text: Assam becomes a Chief Commissioner's province with Sylhet and Cachar; Shillong is the capital.

title: Assam Chief Commissionership
text: The new administration includes Brahmaputra/Surma valley districts and hill districts. Separate regional layers preserve the different hill and princely relationships.

title: Lotha country added
text: The district expands into Lotha country; Wokha becomes an administrative post. The regional context layer enlarges west/north of the earlier stage.

title: Ao country added
text: A further extension brings Ao country into the district. The Mokokchung-region proxy appears; trans-frontier areas are not assigned automatically.

title: Posts and occupation stages
text: The Lunglei post is established in 1889; northern operations and posts follow in the 1889–1890 sequence. Dotted context locates the region without asserting complete control of every village.

title: Separate northern and southern administrations
text: South Lushai Hills is administered from Chittagong; the north is connected to Assam. Aizawl and Lunglei markers distinguish the two centres without inventing their dividing line.

title: Manipur comes under British paramountcy
text: British forces take over in April 1891 and impose the subsequent princely settlement. Hatching now visibly marks British paramountcy while retaining Manipur’s identity. Political oversight through Assam’s Chief Commissioner does not make Manipur an ordinary Assam district.

title: Patharughat
text: Peasants protesting higher land revenue are fired on at Patharughat.

title: Lushai Hills formally incorporated
text: The proclamation of 6 September 1895 formally incorporates the hills. The approximate regional layer becomes solid British colour; this precedes the merger under Assam.

title: The Lushai hills join Assam
text: The northern and southern Lushai administrations merge as a single district under Assam on 1 April; earlier occupation and the 1895 proclamation are separate stages.

title: Unified Lushai district joins Assam
text: The northern and southern administrations merge as one Lushai Hills district under Assam. This is an administrative unification, not the first British expedition.

title: Partition of Bengal
text: Assam is joined to eastern Bengal as the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam (capital Dacca).

title: Eastern Bengal and Assam
text: The new province combines Assam with Dacca, Chittagong, Rajshahi except Darjeeling, and Malda. The map uses qualified modern district groups rather than today’s entire Bangladesh.

title: Assam a province again
text: The partition is reversed; Assam becomes a Chief Commissioner's province again (Governor's province from 1921).

title: Separate Assam administration restored
text: Assam returns to a separate Chief Commissioner’s administration. This changes provincial organisation rather than conquest.

title: The McMahon Line
text: Frontier-tract and McMahon Line context. This does not establish uniform effective British administration throughout present Arunachal Pradesh.

title: Frontier tracts and boundary context
text: The 1914 frontier-tract/boundary episode appears as a dotted regional overlay. It does not imply that every part of modern Arunachal was annexed and effectively administered at once.

title: Quit India in Assam
text: Kanaklata Barua and others are shot leading processions to hoist the flag at police stations.

title: The Battle of Kohima
text: Japanese forces are stopped at Kohima and Imphal, on Assam's eastern edge.

title: Independence and the Sylhet referendum
text: India becomes independent. Sylhet votes to join Pakistan; Karimganj stays in Assam.

title: Manipur accedes to the Dominion of India
text: The Instrument of Accession establishes the relationship with India on specified subjects, including defence, external affairs and communications. Internal government continues before the 1949 merger. Orange hatching distinguishes accession from both British paramountcy and later central administration.

title: Tripura accedes to the Dominion of India
text: The Regent signs the Instrument of Accession on 13 August 1947. Orange hatching shows the relationship with India while internal regency administration continues. The merger and transfer of administration follow in 1949.

title: Indian frontier administration
text: Central responsibility and administration through the Governor of Assam are distinct from ordinary Assam state government.

title: Independence and Sylhet partition
text: Most of historical Sylhet passes to Pakistan, with retained territory in India. Today’s Sylhet division is only a regional proxy here; the detailed award line has not been reconstructed.

title: Manipur transfers administration to India
text: The merger agreement is signed on 21 September and transfers administration to the Dominion of India on 15 October 1949. The map becomes solid Indian colour. This is separate from Assam and precedes Part C constitutional status in 1950.

title: Tripura transfers administration to India
text: The merger agreement is signed on 9 September and transfers administration on 15 October 1949. Solid Indian colour marks central administration. Tripura does not become part of Assam; Part C status follows in 1950.

title: The great earthquake
text: The magnitude-8.6 Assam–Tibet earthquake (15 August 1950) changes the course of rivers in the east.

title: Assam becomes a state
text: The Constitution changes Assam’s status. Neighbouring former princely states and frontier administration remain separate sequences.

title: Manipur becomes an Indian Part C state
text: The Constitution places Manipur among the Part C states from 26 January 1950. This follows the October 1949 transfer of administration and precedes Union Territory status in 1956.

title: Tripura becomes an Indian Part C state
text: The Constitution places Tripura among the Part C states from 26 January 1950. This follows the October 1949 transfer of administration and precedes Union Territory status in 1956.

title: North-East Frontier Agency
text: The frontier administrative reorganisation is shown as a status event without inventing a new international boundary.

title: Manipur becomes a Union Territory
text: Constitutional status changes while the regional outline is retained.

title: Tripura becomes a Union Territory
text: A constitutional status change, distinct from the earlier princely relationship.

title: Naga Hills–Tuensang Area
text: The Naga Hills district and Tuensang frontier area form a separate administrative unit. It is not yet the state of Nagaland.

title: Naga Hills–Tuensang Area separated
text: The separate administrative unit precedes Nagaland’s statehood.

title: Nagaland becomes a state
text: The Naga Hills–Tuensang Area becomes the state of Nagaland.

title: Nagaland statehood
text: Nagaland becomes a state; the event remains a timeline stop even without a new outline.

title: Meghalaya autonomous within Assam
text: An autonomous state is created inside Assam. The context overlay preserves the underlying Assam relationship; the modern outline does not reproduce the period’s Shillong exceptions.

title: Meghalaya autonomy within Assam
text: The autonomous state precedes full statehood by almost two years.

title: Bangladesh is born
text: East Pakistan becomes independent Bangladesh, including Sylhet.

title: The north-east is reorganised
text: Meghalaya becomes a state; Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh become Union Territories (both states in 1987).

title: Meghalaya becomes a state
text: Meghalaya gains full statehood. Its separate solid layer replaces the autonomous-within-Assam context.

title: Mizoram becomes a Union Territory
text: Mizoram leaves Assam as a Union Territory. Its separate statehood event comes later.

title: Manipur becomes a state
text: Manipur gains statehood separately from the Assam territories reorganised by the same Act.

title: Tripura becomes a state
text: Tripura gains full statehood. Its history remains separate from carving territories out of Assam.

title: Arunachal Pradesh becomes a Union Territory
text: The new Union Territory replaces the NEFA arrangement.

title: Northeast reorganisation
text: Meghalaya becomes a state; Mizoram and Arunachal become Union Territories. Manipur and Tripura gain statehood through their own prior constitutional sequences.

title: Dispur becomes the capital
text: Assam's capital moves from Shillong to Dispur in Guwahati.

title: The Assam Movement
text: A six-year agitation against illegal immigration begins, ending with the Assam Accord (1985).

title: The Assam Accord
text: Signed on 15 August 1985 between the movement's leaders and the Government of India.

title: Mizoram becomes a state
text: Full statehood follows the 1986 settlement.

title: Arunachal Pradesh becomes a state
text: Full statehood follows on 20 February 1987.

title: Mizoram and Arunachal statehood
text: Both Union Territories become states on 20 February 1987. Status changes remain navigable even when their map outlines do not change.

title: Bodoland Territorial Council
text: An autonomous council is set up for four districts of the north bank (now the Bodoland Territorial Region).

title: The Moidams become a World Heritage Site
text: The Ahom royal burial mounds at Charaideo are inscribed by UNESCO (July 2024).
